title: Introduction to Computer Networking
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terminology of Introduction to Computer Networking.
Apply introduction to computer networking to a small synthetic example and identify evidence that supports the conclusion.
Identify a relevant limitation or failure mode and describe a safe defensive response.

content.intro: This lesson covers introduction to computer networking in the Networking Fundamentals track. It preserves the PDF's listed subtopics and develops a small, checkable defensive example. You will practice stating scope and assumptions, selecting relevant evidence, and describing what remains uncertain.
content.why_it_matters: Calculate addresses and interpret supplied sample traffic; do not probe networks unless you have explicit authorization. The specific focus here is introduction to computer networking; connect each subtopic to an observable check or a documented decision.

content_blocks.title: Module 03 visual roadmap
content_blocks.alt_text: Module 3 overview for Networking Fundamentals: 9 numbered topic cards arranged in sequence, followed by Learn, Model, Practice safely, Verify, and Document.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Introduction to Computer Networking focuses on what is a network?; lan, wan, wlan, and vpn; network devices and their functions. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case.

items.title: What Is a Network?
items.text: For what is a network?, define the expected behavior, the system or data affected, and the relevant trust boundary. Record a safe verification step and one limitation rather than treating a successful demonstration as proof of complete security.

items.title: LAN, WAN, WLAN, and VPN
items.text: Describe the endpoints, addressing, protocol, direction, and expected behavior before diagnosing a network issue. Use read-only commands, authorized packet captures, and synthetic examples; do not infer compromise from one unusual packet alone.

items.title: Network Devices and Their Functions
items.text: For network devices and their functions, define the expected behavior, the system or data affected, and the relevant trust boundary. Record a safe verification step and one limitation rather than treating a successful demonstration as proof of complete security.

items.title: Network Topologies
items.text: Logs need trustworthy timestamps, useful identity and asset context, retention, access restrictions, and redaction of secrets. A detection rule should have a hypothesis, positive and negative test cases, known blind spots, and an owner.

items.title: Client-Server and Peer-to-Peer Models
items.text: AI-enabled applications add risks around untrusted inputs, data exposure, model and dependency provenance, tool permissions, evaluation, and over-trusting generated output. Keep retrieval and tool actions constrained, minimize sensitive data, and use human review for high-impact decisions.

items.title: Network Segmentation Fundamentals
items.text: Network controls should be tied to an explicit traffic or access policy. Keep rules narrow, log decisions needed for investigations, review exceptions, and test that legitimate business flows still work after changes.

content_blocks.title: Defensive example (synthetic data)
content_blocks.code:
from ipaddress import ip_network

network = ip_network("192.0.2.0/24")  # documentation-only example range
print("network:", network.network_address)
print("prefix length:", network.prefixlen)
print("usable host count:", network.num_addresses - 2)
content_blocks.expected_output:
network: 192.0.2.0
prefix length: 24
usable host count: 254
content_blocks.notes: This example uses synthetic values and has no network dependency. CodeLeaf displays it as instructional text; production does not execute arbitrary learner code.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification
content_blocks.text: Network security becomes easier to reason about when you name the endpoints, protocol, direction, address, and trust boundary of each flow. Before attempting any live security test, obtain explicit permission and verify that the target and method are within scope. When a secure isolated runner is not available, treat the code as a local/synthetic example and do not run arbitrary content on production infrastructure.

content_blocks.title: Run, verify, and reset
content_blocks.text: Review the python snippet as a local calculation. If you choose to run this example, use Python 3 and synthetic inputs in a disposable local environment; compare the displayed expected output with what you observe. If the result differs, check the copied inputs and runtime version, restore the synthetic input, and repeat. No scan, external request, or production change is needed.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Introduction to Computer Networking focuses on what is a network?; lan, wan, wlan, and vpn; network devices and their functions. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case. Apply this to one controlled example, record evidence, and note an important edge case. Next, continue to the next lesson or revisit the prerequisite concept if a key term is unclear.

content.task: Create a concise, reviewable artifact demonstrating Introduction to Computer Networking. Use synthetic data or a controlled local training environment only. Include the relevant syllabus subtopics (What Is a Network?; LAN, WAN, WLAN, and VPN; Network Devices and Their Functions), state assumptions, show what evidence would support your conclusion, identify one failure mode, and recommend a defensive next step. Do not test systems outside written authorization.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use only a synthetic dataset, a disposable local lab, or an explicitly authorized system.
Include a clear scope/assumption statement and enough sanitized evidence for another learner to follow the reasoning.
Explain one limitation, edge case, or failure mode.
Recommend a proportionate defensive control and describe how to verify it safely.
hints: Write the expected behavior and test boundary before looking at a result.
Change one assumption at a time; compare results against the original synthetic case.
Record evidence and uncertainty separately, and select a proportionate protective action.

network: 192.0.2.0
prefix length: 24
usable host count: 254
troubleshooting: The example is illustrative and should be reviewed against current platform/version documentation before production use.
If an output differs, check the input and runtime version; do not broaden the activity to an unrelated system.
Use only fake data and remove all temporary local artifacts when the exercise is complete.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one observation as conclusive proof.
common_mistakes.why: Security telemetry and tests cover only the cases they were designed to observe.
common_mistakes.fix: Corroborate important claims and document coverage gaps.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing a target without confirming authorization.
common_mistakes.why: A technical ability to reach a system does not grant permission to assess it.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic input or a local lab; stop if the approved scope is unclear.

common_mistakes.problem: Skipping the version and context assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Security controls and protocol details vary across implementations and deployment models.
common_mistakes.fix: Record versions, configuration, expected output, and the source used for verification.

summary: Introduction to Computer Networking is best understood within its defined scope and trust boundaries.
Use relevant evidence and test both an expected case and a meaningful failure case.
Record uncertainty and choose a proportionate, authorized defensive next step.

sources.title: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.notes: CSF 2.0 defines outcome-oriented functions and does not prescribe one mandatory implementation. Verify the current CSF resources before publication.

sources.title: CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1
sources.notes: CIS v8.1 aligns control mappings with NIST CSF 2.0. Select safeguards according to context, risk, and operating constraints.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations
sources.notes: Control applicability depends on the organization, system scope, and tailoring decisions.
